newsitem.title: SPAIN: Bonos pare losses but EMU seen clouding outlook.
newsitem.headline: Bonos pare losses but EMU seen clouding outlook.

text.p: Bonos pared losses on Thursday but analysts warn they may be headed for a deeper descent from last week's record peaks as the market took a more cautious view of Spain's European Monetary Union (EMU) prospects.
Government bonds had enjoyed a very strong run-up in recent months on optimism Spain would be among the first countries to qualify for EMU in 1999.
But on Wednesday, the market appeared to succumb to doubts on the chances for the so-called "Club Med" countries -- Italy and Spain -- to make the grade.

Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick said on Thursday Italy and Spain were not likely to be among the first nations to join Europe's planned currency union in 1999. He said they should qualify by 2002.
Also on Thursday, the German central bank's chief economist Otmar Issing warned against efforts by EU members to "window-dress" their economic positions in order to qualify.
"The Bundesbank spoke tough in terms of timing and measures," said Robert Huw, strategist at Natwest in London.

The 10-year spread over German Bunds had more than halved in one year from 440 basis points in September 1995 to a record low of 156 on October 9. It could soon widen to over 200 again, analysts predicted.

At 1130 GMT, the December long-term Bono future was trading at 105.77 after dipping to 105.52 earlier. That compares with an opening on Wednesday of 107.53. Another catalyst for the correction may have been a rise in Swiss money market rates on Wednesday, analysts said.
Large investment funds have been borrowing in Swiss francs to finance long positions in higher-yielding markets such as Italy or Spain, a dealer in London said.

Technical factors provided little support on Thursday though Bonos had recovered from morning lows by midday. Market-watchers said the relief will probably be short-lived and a consolidation is awaited in coming weeks.
"I am afraid more has to come on the consolidation front for Bonos and Btps," said Huw. "They had come so far and so fast."

Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America in Madrid, forecast Bonos will fall another 100 to 200 basis points while the spread over their German counterpart would widen to above the 200 level again in a couple of weeks.
"People think we have already seen the floor and the Bonos are again offering good value. But they are wrong," he said.
With some big players seen unwinding positions in the high yield markets, strategists suggested moving along the curve to shorter-dated securities which still offer good value.
They said a steepening of the yield curve was likely because the short end is suffering less uncertainty.
"The short end is going to perform better in the coming days," said Huw.
Expectations of further reductions in official interest rates because of the benign inflation trend will provide good support for the short end, analysts said.
